Series::CalcAccessor::grad¶

Back to Series::CalcAccessor API Reference

Signature¶

template<class Fn>
Series Series::CalcAccessor::grad(Fn&& fn) const

What It Computes¶

grad() computes the first derivative of a scalar-valued callable with respect to every lane of the owning Series. If x has shape X, fn(x) must be a rank-zero Series and the result has shape X:

gradient[i] = partial fn(x) / partial x[i]

For higher-rank receivers, i is a multi-index. The gradient retains the original axes rather than flattening them into a vector, so its entries remain aligned with the variables they describe.

grad() delegates to the same first-order transform as diff(fn, 1). Its additional value is the scalar-objective check and the resulting shape promise. Use it for losses, energies, likelihoods, and other scalar summaries. Use jac when the callback returns multiple values.

Options And State¶

strict_dependency is honored. Other derivative options do not alter grad()’s fixed first-order, full-gradient geometry: order is ignored and elementwise does not turn a vector objective into a gradient.

The receiver does not need tracks_slope_() and does not receive a stored sensitivity. grad() creates a temporary differentiable leaf, returns a new Series, and preserves the receiver’s dtype-compatible platform.

Examples¶

Example 1. The gradient of a sum of squares is 2x.

auto x = pluss::make_series({2.0, 3.0});
auto gradient = x.calc.grad(
    [](const pluss::Series& z) { return z.square().sum(); });

std::cout << gradient << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[4, 6]

Example 2. Matrix variables remain a matrix. For fn(z) = 1/2 * sum(z^2), the gradient equals z lane by lane.

auto x = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}, {3.0, 4.0}});
auto gradient = x.calc.grad([](const pluss::Series& z) {
  return z.square().mul(0.5).sum();
});

std::cout << gradient << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, 2],
  [3, 4]]

Example 3. grad() and first-order diff() agree for a scalar objective, but grad() communicates the intended geometry directly.

auto x = pluss::make_series({2.0, 3.0});
auto objective = [](const pluss::Series& z) { return z.square().sum(); };

std::cout << "grad=" << x.calc.grad(objective) << "\n";
std::cout << "diff=" << x.calc.diff(objective, 1) << "\n";

Output¶

grad=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[4, 6]
diff=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[4, 6]

Example 4. Returning one value per input lane is not a scalar objective, even when summing it later would have been easy. grad() refuses to guess that reduction.

auto x = pluss::make_series({2.0, 3.0});
try {
  (void)x.calc.grad(
      [](const pluss::Series& z) { return z.square(); });
} catch (const std::exception& error) {
  std::string message = error.what();
  std::cout << message.substr(0, message.find('\n')) << "\n";
}

Output¶

Series.calc.grad: function must return a rank-zero scalar Series

Gradient Flow¶

The returned gradient remains differentiable when every reverse operation on the callback path supports graph construction. This is how higher-order transforms can differentiate a gradient. If only the second derivative is needed, hess expresses that intent and validates the scalar objective in one call.

Failure Modes¶

  • The receiver and callback result must be defined.

  • The callback result must have rank zero; shape [1] is not scalar.

  • Strict dependency mode rejects an objective disconnected from the receiver.

  • Unsupported differentiable paths fail according to the centralized higher-order transform contract.

See Also¶

  • Series::CalcAccessor::jac: first derivative of a non-scalar output.

  • Series::CalcAccessor::hess: second derivative of a scalar objective.
